title: Year two close
hook: the day now begins and ends in the Guru's words; next year, the long story

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukamnama, and your line: one line, kept. Today is the last day of year two.

Day three hundred thirty-two. The Jaap Sahib, for the first time: fast meters, unfamiliar names, praise rolling past faster than you could follow. Since then you've heard the morning prayers, the dusk prayer, the night song, a psalm of peace in twenty-four parts, a ballad for dawn, twelve months of longing, the ninth Guru's calm, and the Ardas, line by line. Somewhere along the way the strangeness wore into something else. Familiar, maybe. Today: amritvela.
screen: `DAY 332: THE JAAP, FOR THE FIRST TIME.` → `A YEAR OF BANIS.` → `STRANGE, THEN FAMILIAR.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of it. Year one gave you the path's words, its stories, its practices and the Japji. Year two gave you a day: the amritvela and the Japji, the Jaap and the Savaiye, Chaupai and Anand, Rehras when work ends, Sohila when the lights go off. Around that day, longer rhythms: Sukhmani for the hard seasons, Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha on the first of each month, the ninth Guru's saloks near the Granth's close, and the Ardas, said standing, at the start and end of gatherings and undertakings. Why does this matter so much to Sikhs? Guru Ram Das gives an answer in a hymn on Ang 982: the bani is the Guru, and the Guru is the bani, and within the bani is all the nectar. For Sikhs, if the words are the Guru, then a day spent in the words is a day spent in the Guru's company. That's what the daily banis are, seen from the inside: not a list of tasks, but company, from before dawn to after dark. It explains the week behind you, too, when the Granth itself was named Guru. Now turn and face the other way. Year three is the long story: Sikh history told slowly, beginning with its first tellers. Tomorrow you meet Bhai Gurdas, who wrote out the Adi Granth in his own hand for Guru Arjan and composed forty vars of his own. After him comes Bhai Nand Lal, a poet who sat with the Tenth Guru. The voices you learned this year become the voices in that story. When the Gurus speak in year three, you'll already know how they sound.
screen: `YEAR TWO: A DAY IN THE GURU'S WORDS.` · `THE LONGER RHYTHMS AROUND THE DAY.` · `THE BANI IS THE GURU.` · `YEAR THREE: THE LONG STORY.` · then, large: `THE DAY, IN HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and let the year settle like dust in a quiet room. Then picture tomorrow morning, just after you wake, with the line you kept yesterday, or one word, Waheguru, arriving first, before the to-do list and the news. If you pray, that word can be the first thing you say tomorrow; if you don't, simply let the morning have a little room in it.
Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn when the day begins in the Guru's words: the end of the daily banis this year, with year three's long story ahead.
Your line: the day, in his words. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs begin the day at amritvela with the morning banis and end it with Kirtan Sohila, understanding the bani itself as the Guru whose company they keep through the day.

fork.setup: the day is ending, and Sikhs say the bani is the Guru. which bani do many Sikhs say last thing at night?
fork.reveal: Kirtan Sohila is the night song; the same words that close a day also close a life at Sikh funerals.

trapdoor: what you thought: daily prayers are a set of tasks to tick off.
what it means: for Sikhs the words are the Guru, so a day in them is a day in the Guru's company.
what a scholar hears: Guru Ram Das's line in Raga Nat (Ang 982) makes bani and Guru one, which Sikhs see as the ground on which Guru Gobind Singh later passed the guruship to the Granth in 1708.

chat.says: Why do Sikhs fill the whole day with prayers, from before dawn to bedtime?
options: For Sikhs, the bani is the Guru: a day in the words is the Guru's company.
Every prayer missed counts against you, so the whole day has to be filled.
To keep the mind so busy there's no time left over for ordinary life.
chat.meaning: On Ang 982 Guru Ram Das sings that the bani is the Guru and the Guru is the bani. So for Sikhs, the daily banis are company, not tasks.
